newsitem.title: USA: February data to dictate open for U.S. stocks.
newsitem.headline: February data to dictate open for U.S. stocks.

text.p: Wall Street stocks will take their cue Friday from the Producer Price Index for February, after concerns about interest rates triggered a 160-point drop in the Dow yesterday.
February PPI is due at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, and industrial production and capacity utilization are due at 0915 EST/1415 GMT.
"If the numbers are okay we will attempt a bit of a bounce, led by Philip Morris, in the Dow," said Larry Wachtel, analyst at Prudential Securities.
"Philip Morris was one-quarter of the decline yesterday, and if you can get a bounce in Philip Morris shares and few other Dow stocks, you will have a decent opening," he said.
Philip Morris bounced 1-1/2 to 127-1/2 in London after sliding 11-1/2 in New York Thursday. Shares in RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp climbed 1/2 in London to 33-3/4 after a drop of 2-7/8 in New York.
Tobacco shares were hit hard Thursday on news that the Mississippi Supreme Court had rejected a challenge to the state's Medicaid suit against tobacco companies.

"This whole market advance was based on a Goldilocks scenario -- the economy is not too strong, not too weak," Wachtel said. "Now, you have an economy which is too strong and reaching a four percent annual growth rate.

"The history of the stock market in recent years has seen the Dow bouncing after dips. People buy on dips because the market is so elevated. But the Dow is certainly entitled to more of a correction."
U.S. financial markets plunged Thursday amid growing expectations that the Federal Open Market Committee will nudge interest rates higher when it meets on March 25.
In Tokyo the Nikkei Average was up 23.16 points, or 0.13 percent, to 17,923.64.
In London the FTSE 100 Index was down 20.7 at 4377.0.
U.S. stocks staged a moderate recovery in London, with most shares recouping 1/8 to 1/4 from their New York closing levels.
The dollar was firmer against the mark in Europe and was strong against the yen in Tokyo.
U.S. Treasuries were slightly higher, with the long bond up 1/32 to yield 6.96 percent.

The Wall Street Journal's "Heard on the Street" column said some investors claim to have had success buying the Dow's so-called dogs at the end of each year, holding them for a year and then repeating the excercise.

The New York Times's "Market Place"column said that if the Dow had made the stock changes announced this week back in 1991, the last time the index was adjusted, this week would have seen the Dow come close to 8,000.
